optionExplanations: Cervical medullaris lesions affect all limbs and present with upper motor neuron signs, not localized lower limb hyporeflexia.
Lower-thoracic cord involvement causes symmetrical weakness and increased reflexes, unlike the asymmetrical findings in cauda equina.
Mid-thoracic spinal cord compression would typically cause upper motor neuron signs like hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses.
Conus medullaris typically presents with a mix of signs, often including increased knee reflexes but decreased ankle reflexes.
Cauda equina syndrome results in lower motor neuron signs, characterized by decreased or absent reflexes and a flexor plantar response.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 142 (Book Page): [Table 7.13] Cauda equina... Reflexes: Decreased knee and ankle reflexes with flexor plantar reflex.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
coreConcept: Diagnostic significance of the Sister Mary Joseph nodule
statement: A 68-year-old female presents with a three-month history of progressive abdominal bloating, early satiety, and a 12 kg weight loss. Physical examination reveals a firm, irregular mass in the epigastrium and a palpable, non-tender nodule at the umbilicus. Based on these clinical signs, which primary malignancy is most highly suspected?
optionExplanations: Thyroid cancer typically spreads to local lymph nodes or bone; abdominal umbilical metastasis is not a recognized clinical hallmark.
An umbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) is a classic sign of intra-abdominal malignancy, most commonly gastric or ovarian cancer.
Renal cell carcinoma presents with a renal mass or hematuria; while it can metastasize, gastric/ovarian origins are far more common for this sign.
Lung cancer commonly presents with clubbing or SVCO signs, but abdominal umbilical nodules are not a classic feature of its spread.
Breast cancer metastasizes to bone, lung, and liver, but rarely presents with a primary umbilical (Sister Mary Joseph) nodule.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [Clinical examination of the cancer patient] Abdomen... Umbilical nodule... Ascites (ovarian carcinoma) Page 136 (Book Page): Signet-ring cells favour a gastric primary.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
coreConcept: Clinical features of hypercalcemia of malignancy
statement: A patient with known breast cancer presents with severe constipation, polyuria, and polydipsia. Laboratory investigations confirm an elevated serum calcium level. Which additional clinical feature is most likely to be present on examination?
optionExplanations: Constipation in hypercalcemia is due to decreased smooth muscle contractility, which manifests as hypoactive or absent bowel sounds.
Enhanced muscle irritability (tetany) is a sign of hypocalcemia, not the hypercalcemia typically found in metastatic breast cancer.
Hypercalcemia often causes neurological symptoms ranging from mild drowsiness to severe delirium and coma due to central nervous system depression.
A positive Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm) indicates latent tetany associated with hypocalcemia or hypomagnesemia.
Hypercalcemia typically results in depressed or diminished deep tendon reflexes, whereas hypocalcemia causes hyperreflexia.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 144 (Book Page): The symptoms of hypercalcaemia... include drowsiness, delirium, nausea and vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia and dehydration.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 72-year-old male with metastatic prostate cancer is assessed during a routine clinic visit. He reports that he is capable of all self-care but is unable to carry out any work. He spends approximately six hours of his 16-hour waking day resting in bed. What is his ECOG performance status?
optionExplanations: Grade 2 indicates the patient is ambulatory and capable of self-care but unable to work; they are awake for more than 50% of the day.
Grade 1 indicates restriction in strenuous activity but the patient is still able to carry out light work or sedentary occupations.
Grade 4 indicates the patient is completely disabled, unable to carry out any self-care, and totally confined to bed or chair.
Grade 0 indicates the patient is fully active and able to carry on all usual activities without any restrictions.
Grade 3 describes a patient capable of only limited self-care, confined to bed or chair more than 50% of waking hours.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 137 (Book Page): [Table 7.6] 2... Ambulatory and capable of all self-care but unable to work. Up and about more than 50% of waking hours

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 55-year-old male with a significant smoking history presents with darkening and thickening of the skin in his axillary and cervical regions. The skin appears velvety in texture. This clinical sign is most commonly associated with which underlying malignancy?
optionExplanations: Acanthosis nigricans (velvety skin thickening) is a classic paraneoplastic sign of internal malignancy, most notably gastric adenocarcinoma.
Melanoma is associated with vitiligo as a paraneoplastic sign, rather than the hyperpigmented velvety plaques of acanthosis nigricans.
Small cell lung cancer is more famously associated with Lambert-Eaton syndrome or ectopic ACTH, not typically acanthosis nigricans.
Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with erythrocytosis due to ectopic erythropoietin production rather than acanthosis nigricans.
Lymphomas are frequently associated with pruritus or pemphigus, while acanthosis nigricans is linked to gastrointestinal tract cancers.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 139 (Book Page): [Table 7.10] Acanthosis nigricans... Gastric, oesophageal cancer

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
coreConcept: Early clinical signs of malignant spinal cord compression
statement: A 60-year-old man presents with a 'band-like' pain across his mid-thorax that worsens when he coughs or lies flat. He has a known history of advanced prostate cancer. On examination, there is symmetrical weakness in his lower limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings?
optionExplanations: Lambert-Eaton involves proximal muscle weakness that improves with use, not acute spinal pain exacerbated by coughing.
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy presents with wrist tenderness and finger clubbing, not with neurological deficits or band-like back pain.
Malignant spinal cord compression classically presents with 'band-like' pain exacerbated by coughing and lying flat, followed by leg weakness.
SVCO presents with facial edema and venous distension in the neck and chest, not with localized radicular back pain or leg weakness.
Cerebellar degeneration presents with ataxia and coordination issues rather than localized spinal pain and symmetrical lower limb motor weakness.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 141 (Book Page): The earliest sign is back pain, often rapidly worsening or in a ‘band’, most marked on coughing and lying flat.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
coreConcept: Clinical signs of Hypertrophic Pulmonary Osteoarthropathy (HPOA)
statement: During a clinical examination of a 58-year-old heavy smoker with a persistent cough, the physician notes swelling and tenderness of the wrists and ankles. Finger clubbing is also present. Which physiological finding is most likely to be confirmed on a skeletal survey?
options: Lytic lesions of the long bones
optionExplanations: Diffuse osteopenia is a generalized metabolic bone finding and is not the specific pathology underlying the joint tenderness of HPOA.
Blastic lesions are characteristic of metastatic prostate cancer and usually involve the axial skeleton rather than the distal joints.
Lytic lesions are typical of multiple myeloma or metastatic breast cancer but do not cause the specific wrist tenderness seen in HPOA.
Hypertrophic Pulmonary Osteoarthropathy (HPOA) is characterized by clubbing and subperiosteal new bone formation, often presenting as wrist tenderness.
Multiple fractures may occur in advanced cancer with bone metastases, but they present with focal bone tenderness rather than symmetric joint swelling.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Wrist tenderness (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy)

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
coreConcept: Clinical signs of ectopic hormone production
statement: A patient with a mediastinal mass is found to have hypertension and a 'moon-shaped' face on examination. These clinical signs are most suggestive of which paraneoplastic phenomenon?
optionExplanations: Ectopic ACTH production, common in small cell lung cancer, leads to Cushing’s syndrome, characterized by a 'moon face' and hypertension.
SIADH causes hyponatremia and fluid retention but does not produce the fat redistribution or hypertension seen in Cushingoid presentations.
Ectopic insulin production causes hypoglycemia and related symptoms (confusion, sweating) rather than the signs of hypercortisolism.
Excessive erythropoietin results in polycythemia and plethora, not the fat deposits and skin changes associated with Cushingoid features.
PTHrP causes hypercalcemia, leading to symptoms like polyuria and constipation, rather than the physical features of steroid excess.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [Clinical examination of the cancer patient] Face... Cushingoid features Page 144 (Book Page): [Table 7.18] ACTH... Cushing’s syndrome... SCLC

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 62-year-old male with a history of chronic weight loss and dyspepsia presents with a firm, non-tender nodule at the umbilicus. Physical examination also reveals hepatomegaly and a hard epigastric mass. What is the most likely clinical significance of this umbilical finding?
options: It indicates a benign herniation of the omentum through the ring
It suggests localized inflammation from a ruptured gastric ulcer
It represents a primary urachal carcinoma of the abdominal wall
It is a characteristic finding of primary peritoneal mesothelioma
It is a cutaneous metastasis from an intra-abdominal malignancy
correctOption: It is a cutaneous metastasis from an intra-abdominal malignancy
optionExplanations: While umbilical hernias are common, a firm, non-tender nodule in an oncology patient strongly suggests the Sister Mary Joseph sign.
Inflammatory nodules from ulcers are typically tender and associated with acute peritoneal signs, not a chronic epigastric mass.
Urachal carcinoma is a rare primary tumor but does not typically present as a discrete umbilical nodule in the context of an epigastric mass.
While mesothelioma causes peritoneal spread, the umbilical nodule is specifically associated with various adenocarcinomas as a metastatic sign.
An umbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) is a classic clinical sign of metastatic spread from an intra-abdominal or pelvic malignancy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Umbilical nodule... [Page 150 (Book Page)] Occasionally, peritoneal deposits are palpable as an omental ‘cake’ and nodules in the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph nodules).

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 58-year-old heavy smoker presents with a chronic cough and recent onset of bilateral wrist pain and swelling. On examination, there is noticeable thickening of the distal radius and ulna with associated tenderness. Which clinical entity is most likely associated with these findings?
options: Metastatic infiltration of the synovial membranes of the wrist joints
Paraneoplastic syndrome known as hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
Direct invasion of the brachial plexus by a superior sulcus tumor
Chronic renal failure resulting in secondary hyperparathyroid bone disease
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome causing referred distal joint pain
correctOption: Paraneoplastic syndrome known as hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
optionExplanations: Metastatic joint involvement is rare compared to paraneoplastic syndromes like HPOA in lung cancer patients.
Wrist tenderness and swelling in a lung cancer context (often with finger clubbing) is a classic sign of HPOA.
Brachial plexus invasion (Pancoast tumor) typically causes neurological deficits and shoulder pain, not bilateral wrist tenderness.
While renal failure affects bones, the presentation in a smoker with respiratory symptoms points toward a pulmonary paraneoplastic process.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome primarily affects the neuromuscular junction, leading to proximal muscle weakness rather than distal bone tenderness.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Wrist tenderness (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy)

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A patient presents with bilateral lower limb weakness and sensory loss. On neurological examination, the clinician notes increased knee and ankle reflexes with an extensor plantar response. According to the standard clinical differentiation of neurological deficits in oncology, which location is the lesion most likely situated?
options: Thoracic region of the spinal cord
Peripheral nerves of the lower limbs
Conus medullaris of the spinal cord
Cauda equina at the lumbar level
correctOption: Thoracic region of the spinal cord
optionExplanations: Upper motor neuron signs (increased reflexes and extensor plantars) are characteristic of spinal cord compression above the conus, often in the thoracic region.
Peripheral nerve lesions cause lower motor neuron signs, such as decreased or absent reflexes, not increased reflexes.
Conus medullaris lesions often present with increased knee reflexes but decreased ankle reflexes.
Cauda equina syndrome results in decreased knee and ankle reflexes and flexor plantar responses.
Neuromuscular junction disorders like Lambert-Eaton affect strength but do not produce extensor plantar responses.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 141 (Book Page): [Box 7.13] Spinal cord: Weakness: Symmetrical and profound; Reflexes: Increased (or absent) knee and ankle reflexes with extensor plantar reflex.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 67-year-old male with a history of small cell lung cancer presents with progressive facial puffiness and a feeling of 'fullness' in his head that worsens when he bends over. Physical examination reveals distended, non-pulsatile neck veins and dusky skin coloration over the chest. Which finding would most likely confirm the clinical diagnosis of Superior Vena Cava Obstruction (SVCO)?
options: Development of venous collateral vessels over the anterior chest wall
Visible pulsations of the internal jugular vein at 45 degrees
A paradoxical rise in the jugular venous pressure during inspiration
A sharp 'y' descent visible on the jugular venous pressure waveform
Resolution of facial edema when the patient remains in a flat position
correctOption: Development of venous collateral vessels over the anterior chest wall
optionExplanations: The presence of chest wall collaterals and non-pulsatile venous distension are key clinical hallmarks of SVCO.
Pulsatile neck veins suggest heart failure or tricuspid issues; SVCO causes non-pulsatile distension because the obstruction is proximal to the heart.
Kussmaul's sign is associated with constrictive pericarditis, not primarily with extrinsic compression of the SVC.
A sharp 'y' descent is a feature of the JVP in conditions like constrictive pericarditis or tricuspid regurgitation.
In SVCO, lying flat or bending over increases the back-flow pressure, worsening the edema and symptoms rather than resolving them.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 142 (Book Page): [Box 7.15] Venous distension of chest wall (54%)... Page 142 (Book Page): Collateral vessels may develop over a period of weeks and the flow of blood in the collaterals helps to confirm the diagnosis.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: During the physical examination of a patient with suspected apical lung carcinoma, the clinician observes unilateral miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis. What is the specific clinical name for this sign and its anatomical cause in this patient?
options: Superior Vena Cava syndrome due to compression of the subclavian vein
Lambert-Eaton syndrome due to antibodies against calcium channels
Cushingoid feature due to ectopic adrenocorticotrophic hormone secretion
Trousseau sign due to migratory thrombophlebitis in a prothrombotic state
Horner syndrome due to compression of the cervical sympathetic chain
correctOption: Horner syndrome due to compression of the cervical sympathetic chain
optionExplanations: SVCO causes facial edema and venous distension, not the specific sympathetic triad of Horner syndrome.
Lambert-Eaton causes muscle weakness; it does not typically present with the miosis and ptosis triad of Horner syndrome.
Cushingoid features include a moon face and central obesity, not the focal ocular findings described.
Trousseau sign refers to migratory thrombophlebitis, often associated with pancreatic cancer, unrelated to ocular signs.
Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) results from the interruption of the sympathetic supply, often by a Pancoast tumor at the lung apex.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Horner syndrome [under Face category]

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 45-year-old male presents for a screening exam. The examiner notes a firm, enlarged, non-tender lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa. Which anatomical terminology is most appropriate for this clinical finding and what does it commonly signal?
options: Delphian node; indicates an advanced metastatic laryngeal carcinoma
Virchow’s node; indicates metastasis from a subdiaphragmatic primary
Osler node; indicates systemic emboli from infectious endocarditis
Sister Mary Joseph node; indicates metastatic colorectal cancer
Epitrochlear node; indicates localized infection of the upper extremity
correctOption: Virchow’s node; indicates metastasis from a subdiaphragmatic primary
optionExplanations: The Delphian node is a midline prelaryngeal node associated with thyroid or laryngeal pathology, not the supraclavicular fossa.
Virchow's node is a left supraclavicular lymph node that is a classic site for metastasis from gastric or other abdominal cancers.
Osler nodes are painful, red nodules on the pads of fingers/toes seen in endocarditis.
Sister Mary Joseph node is located at the umbilicus, not the supraclavicular fossa.
Epitrochlear nodes are located near the elbow, not the supraclavicular area.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Lymph nodes... Supraclavicular

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: In a patient with a known history of metastatic breast cancer, physical examination of the chest reveals stony dullness on percussion and absent breath sounds at the right base. Tactile vocal fremitus is decreased. What is the most likely pathological sign being identified?
options: Interstitial fibrosis following high-dose bleomycin chemotherapy
Pericardial effusion with associated cardiomegaly and tamponade
Lobar consolidation secondary to post-obstructive pneumonia
Pneumothorax due to spontaneous rupture of a pleural bleb
Malignant pleural effusion involving the basal pleural space
correctOption: Malignant pleural effusion involving the basal pleural space
optionExplanations: Fibrosis typically causes fine end-inspiratory crackles and is not associated with stony dullness.
Pericardial effusion affects the heart sounds and JVP but does not typically cause stony dull percussion over the lung bases.
Consolidation typically presents with increased vocal fremitus and bronchial breath sounds, not absent sounds.
Pneumothorax would present with hyper-resonance on percussion rather than stony dullness.
Stony dullness, absent breath sounds, and decreased fremitus are the classic physical examination findings for a pleural effusion.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Respiratory: Pleural effusion... Page 145 (Book Page): This is a common complication of cancer and 40% of all pleural effusions are due to malignancy.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 70-year-old female with advanced multiple myeloma presents to the clinic with profound dehydration, confusion, and generalized muscle weakness. She complains of severe constipation and frequent urination. Her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg and skin turgor is poor. Which metabolic emergency is most consistent with these clinical signs?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
Ectopic production of erythropoietin leading to polycythemia
Tumor lysis syndrome following the start of chemotherapy
Hypercalcemia of malignancy causing renal concentrating defects
Hypoglycemia caused by ectopic insulin production from the tumor
correctOption: Hypercalcemia of malignancy causing renal concentrating defects
optionExplanations: SIADH causes hyponatremia and fluid retention, not dehydration and polyuria.
Erythropoietin excess would cause hyperviscosity symptoms, not the constellation of polyuria and constipation.
Tumor lysis syndrome typically presents with hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, and renal failure symptoms, but polyuria is not a standard early feature.
Hypercalcemia commonly presents with 'stones, bones, abdominal moans (constipation), and psychic groans (confusion)' along with polyuria and dehydration.
Hypoglycemia would cause sweating, tachycardia, and altered consciousness but not polyuria or constipation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 143 (Book Page): Symptoms [of hypercalcaemia]... include drowsiness, delirium, nausea and vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia and dehydration.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
coreConcept: Acanthosis Nigricans as a paraneoplastic sign
statement: A 55-year-old female presents with hyperpigmented, velvety plaques in the axillae and on the neck. She has also noted unintentional weight loss over the last three months. Which paraneoplastic clinical sign is being described and with which malignancy is it most strongly associated?
options: Vitiligo; associated with metastatic malignant melanoma
Pemphigus; associated with Kaposi’s sarcoma or lymphoma
Dermatomyositis; associated with ovarian or small cell lung cancer
Acanthosis nigricans; associated with follicular thyroid carcinoma
Acanthosis nigricans; associated with gastric adenocarcinoma
correctOption: Acanthosis nigricans; associated with gastric adenocarcinoma
optionExplanations: Vitiligo is associated with melanoma but presents as depigmented (white) patches, not dark velvety plaques.
Pemphigus involves blistering of the skin and mucous membranes.
Dermatomyositis presents with a heliotrope rash and proximal muscle weakness, not velvety plaques.
While Acanthosis nigricans is the correct sign, its classic oncological association is with gastrointestinal (especially gastric) cancers, not thyroid cancer.
Acanthosis nigricans is a paraneoplastic sign characterized by dark, velvety skin changes, most classically associated with gastric cancer.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 139 (Book Page): [Box 7.10] Acanthosis nigricans: Gastric, oesophageal cancer

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: On inspection of a cancer patient’s hands, the clinician notes clubbing and 'nicotine staining.' What is the clinical significance of noting 'nicotine staining' during an oncological physical examination?
options: It indicates a specific vitamin deficiency common in cancer cachexia
It is a side effect of cytotoxic drugs like 5-fluorouracil or cisplatin
It represents cutaneous deposition of porphyrins from liver metastases
It serves as a marker for high-risk behavior linked to lung and throat cancer
It is a pathognomonic sign for the presence of a carcinoid tumor
correctOption: It serves as a marker for high-risk behavior linked to lung and throat cancer
optionExplanations: Staining is external from tobacco smoke, not a metabolic result of cachexia.
Cytotoxics can cause skin changes (like palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia), but the yellow-brown staining of fingers is from smoking.
Porphyrin deposition is related to porphyria, not the clinical 'tobacco staining' found on the hands of heavy smokers.
Nicotine staining (signs of smoking) is a crucial clinical observation indicating exposure to a major carcinogen for several cancers.
Carcinoid tumors have specific signs like flushing and diarrhea, not nicotine staining of the hands.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Hands: Clubbing, Signs of smoking

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 62-year-old male smoker is being evaluated for progressive weight loss and a persistent cough. During the abdominal examination, a firm, non-tender, palpable mass is identified at the umbilicus. This specific clinical finding is most strongly associated with which of the following?
options: Congenital failure of the umbilical ring to close fully
Superficial bruising from acute necrotizing pancreatitis
Secondary spread from an intra-abdominal malignancy
A primary ventral hernia containing incarcerated fat
Dilation of paraumbilical veins from portal hypertension
correctOption: Secondary spread from an intra-abdominal malignancy
optionExplanations: Congenital umbilical hernias are usually seen in children and do not present as firm nodules associated with cancer-related constitutional symptoms.
Superficial bruising around the umbilicus is Cullen's sign, associated with retroperitoneal hemorrhage in pancreatitis, not a metastatic nodule.
A palpable umbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) typically represents cutaneous metastasis from an internal malignancy, most commonly gastrointestinal or pelvic cancers.
While a hernia can present as an umbilical mass, it is typically soft, reducible, or painful if incarcerated, rather than a firm metastatic nodule.
Dilated paraumbilical veins (caput medusae) result from portal hypertension and appear as tortuous vessels rather than a discrete nodular mass.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Umbilical nodule... Mass in epigastrium... Abdominal distension... Ascites... Hepatomegaly... Splenomegaly... Renal mass... Pelvic or adnexal mass

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 58-year-old woman with a mediastinal mass presents with facial swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck veins, and plethora of the face and arms. Which physiological mechanism primarily accounts for these clinical manifestations?
options: Reduced right ventricular filling due to pericardial effusion
Infiltration of the sympathetic chain by a malignant growth
Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system axis
Extrinsic compression of the superior vena cava by a tumor
Impaired drainage of the thoracic duct leading to chylothorax
correctOption: Extrinsic compression of the superior vena cava by a tumor
optionExplanations: While pericardial effusions occur in cancer, they cause muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus rather than localized upper body plethora and distended arm veins.
Infiltration of the sympathetic chain leads to Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), not the vascular congestion seen in SVCO.
RAAS activation causes generalized fluid retention and systemic hypertension rather than localized venous congestion of the upper body.
SVCO leads to increased venous pressure in the upper body, resulting in the classic presentation of facial edema, plethora, and distended neck/chest veins.
Thoracic duct obstruction typically leads to chylous effusions in the pleural space rather than superficial venous distension and facial plethora.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 143 (Book Page): Superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO) is a common complication of cancer that can occur through extrinsic compression or intravascular blockage. The most common causes of extrinsic compression are lung cancer, lymphoma and metastatic tumours

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: During the musculoskeletal examination of a patient with suspected bronchogenic carcinoma, the clinician notes bilateral clubbing and elicited tenderness upon palpation of the wrists and distal forearms. What is the most likely clinical significance of this combination of findings?
options: Metastatic infiltration of the distal radius and ulna bones
Paraneoplastic syndrome of hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
Rheumatoid arthritis occurring as a coincident comorbid condition
Osteomalacia secondary to tumor-induced fibroblast growth factor-23
Cushingoid skeletal changes from ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone
correctOption: Paraneoplastic syndrome of hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
optionExplanations: Bone metastases usually present as focal, severe pain in the spine or pelvis rather than bilateral symmetric wrist tenderness and finger clubbing.
HPOA is a paraneoplastic syndrome classically seen in lung cancer, characterized by the triad of clubbing, periostitis of long bones (causing wrist/ankle pain), and arthritis.
While rheumatoid arthritis causes wrist pain, it does not typically cause the specific digital clubbing seen in pulmonary malignancies.
FGF-23 production causes hypophosphatemic osteomalacia, leading to generalized bone pain and fractures, but not the specific sign of finger clubbing.
Ectopic ACTH causes features of Cushing syndrome like buffalo hump and moon facies, but skeletal involvement is primarily osteoporosis, not periostitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Wrist tenderness (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy)... Finger clubbing in lung cancer

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
coreConcept: Conus Medullaris vs Cauda Equina Syndrome
statement: A 74-year-old male with known metastatic prostate cancer presents with a three-day history of worsening lower back pain described as 'band-like' around his waist. On examination, he has symmetrical lower limb weakness, saddle anesthesia, and early loss of bladder control. Which of the following is the most likely neuroanatomical site of involvement?
options: Cervical spinal cord at the level of the C5-C6 vertebrae
Thoracic spinal cord at the level of the T4-T8 vertebrae
Cauda equina consisting of the lumbar and sacral nerve roots
Bilateral lumbosacral plexus due to bulky pelvic lymphadenopathy
Conus medullaris at the termination of the spinal cord
correctOption: Conus medullaris at the termination of the spinal cord
optionExplanations: Cervical lesions would cause upper limb signs and a sensory level on the trunk, not the localized saddle anesthesia and band-like waist pain described.
Thoracic spinal cord compression presents with a clear sensory level and late sphincter loss compared to the early loss seen in terminal cord lesions.
Cauda equina syndrome typically presents with asymmetrical weakness and later onset of sphincter loss compared to conus medullaris lesions.
Lumbosacral plexopathy usually presents with asymmetrical nerve root distribution pain and motor deficits rather than symmetrical saddle anesthesia and early bladder loss.
Conus medullaris syndrome is characterized by early sphincter disturbance (urinary retention/fecal incontinence), symmetrical weakness, and saddle anesthesia.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 142 (Book Page): Comparison of features of neurological deficit... Conus medullaris... Symmetrical and variable weakness, Increased knee reflex, decreased ankle reflex, extensor plantar reflex, Symmetrical saddle distribution sensory loss, Early loss of sphincters

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 55-year-old man being treated for lung adenocarcinoma presents with a prominent acneiform rash localized to his face and upper back. This physical finding is most characteristically a side effect of which targeted therapy class?
options: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) inhibitors
optionExplanations: PARP inhibitors are most commonly associated with hematological toxicities like anemia and neutropenia, not acneiform rashes.
CDK4/6 inhibitors (e.g., palbociclib) predominantly cause neutropenia and gastrointestinal upset rather than the specific acneiform rash typical of EGFR inhibitors.
EGFR inhibitors (e.g., erlotinib, cetuximab) classically cause a papulopustular (acneiform) rash, which often correlates with treatment efficacy.
VEGF inhibitors are more associated with hypertension, proteinuria, and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (hand-foot syndrome) rather than acneiform rashes.
HER2 inhibitors like trastuzumab are primarily associated with cardiotoxicity (cardiomyopathy) rather than specific acneiform skin eruptions.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): Acneiform rashes – EGFR inhibitors... Paronychia – EGFR inhibitors... Finger tip cracks – EGFR inhibitors... Trichomegaly – EGFR inhibitors

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 68-year-old patient with advanced gastric cancer is being assessed for treatment fitness. The patient is ambulatory and capable of all self-care but is unable to carry out any work activities. He spends approximately 30% of his waking hours resting in bed. What is his ECOG performance status?
optionExplanations: Grade 2 describes a patient who is ambulatory and capable of all self-care but unable to work; they are up and about more than 50% of waking hours.
Grade 1 applies to patients restricted in physically strenuous activity but ambulatory and able to carry out light work.
Grade 3 applies to patients capable of only limited self-care and confined to a bed or chair more than 50% of waking hours.
Grade 4 signifies a completely disabled patient who cannot carry out any self-care and is totally confined to a bed or chair.
Grade 0 signifies a fully active patient who can carry on all pre-disease performance without restriction.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 137 (Book Page): 2 Ambulatory and capable of all self-care but unable to work. Up and about more than 50% of waking hours

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 60-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer to the bones presents with progressive drowsiness, nausea, and frequent urination. On physical examination, she appears severely dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. Which metabolic abnormality is the most likely cause of these clinical signs?
options: Hyperkalemia secondary to rapid tumor cell turnover
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
Hypercalcemia resulting from increased bone resorption
Hyponatremia due to ectopic vasopressin production
Hypoglycemia from insulin-like growth factor secretion
correctOption: Hypercalcemia resulting from increased bone resorption
optionExplanations: Hyperkalemia is associated with cardiac arrhythmias and muscle weakness but does not typically present with the polyuria-dehydration complex.
SIADH causes hyponatremia and fluid retention, leading to signs of fluid overload or normal volume status, not severe dehydration and polyuria.
Hypercalcemia (often due to PTHrP or bone metastases) causes a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus-like state leading to polyuria, polydipsia, and subsequent dehydration.
Ectopic vasopressin causes hyponatremia and concentrated urine, which would not explain the polyuria and severe clinical dehydration observed.
Hypoglycemia would present with autonomic symptoms (sweating, tremors) and neuroglycopenia, not polyuria and dehydration.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 144 (Book Page): The symptoms of hypercalcaemia are often non-specific and may mimic those of the underlying malignancy. They include drowsiness, delirium, nausea and vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia and dehydration.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 65-year-old man with a long history of smoking presents with severe proximal muscle weakness that improves significantly with repeated exercise. He also reports a dry mouth and erectile dysfunction. Chest imaging reveals a small central mass. Which of the following paraneoplastic features is he demonstrating?
optionExplanations: Acanthosis nigricans is a skin marker (hyperpigmented velvety plaques) associated with gastric cancer, not a neuromuscular junction disorder.
Dermatomyositis presents with proximal weakness but is typically associated with skin signs (Gottron papules, heliotrope rash) and does not improve with repeated effort.
Cerebellar degeneration presents with ataxia, dysarthria, and nystagmus, rather than the fatigable muscle weakness seen here.
Myasthenia gravis causes weakness that worsens with activity (the opposite of LEMS) and is associated with thymoma, not small cell lung cancer.
LEMS is a paraneoplastic syndrome of Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) characterized by proximal muscle weakness that improves with use, and autonomic features like dry mouth.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 139 (Book Page): Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome... Small cell lung cancer... Page 145 (Book Page): Antibodies to pre-synaptic calcium channels (Lambert–Eaton syndrome)

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A patient with bulky Burkitt lymphoma is started on intensive cytotoxic chemotherapy. Within 18 hours, he develops a cardiac arrhythmia and muscular twitching. Regular monitoring of which biochemical marker would have provided the earliest indicator of this treatment-related syndrome?
optionExplanations: Hyperuricemia is a key feature of TLS but potassium is released more rapidly from the cytoplasm during the initial phase of cell lysis.
Hyperkalemia is the earliest biochemical marker of Tumor Lysis Syndrome as potassium is the primary intracellular cation released immediately upon cell death.
Albumin levels are generally unaffected or low in cancer patients; they are not a marker for the acute metabolic crisis of tumor lysis syndrome.
Hypocalcemia occurs in TLS due to phosphate binding, but it is typically a secondary effect following the initial rise in intracellular ions like potassium.
In TLS, serum phosphate levels increase (hyperphosphatemia) due to release from lysed tumor cells, not decrease.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 144 (Book Page): Tumour lysis syndrome... Cellular destruction results in the release of potassium, phosphate, nucleic acids and purines... Elevated serum potassium may be the earliest biochemical marker

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: An 82-year-old male presents with right-sided miosis, mild ptosis, and a lack of sweating on the right side of his face. Chest X-ray reveals a mass in the apex of the right lung. Which clinical sign is this constellation of findings termed?
optionExplanations: Cushing syndrome results from glucocorticoid excess (e.g., ectopic ACTH) and presents with weight gain, moon facies, and purple striae.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome is a neuromuscular disorder causing muscle weakness, not the specific ocular and autonomic signs described.
Superior Vena Cava (SVC) syndrome presents with facial and neck swelling and venous distension, not miosis and ptosis.
Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) results from sympathetic chain interruption, often by an apical lung (Pancoast) tumor.
Trousseau syndrome refers to migratory thrombophlebitis associated with malignancy (especially pancreatic), not neurological findings.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Face... Conjunctival pallor... Icterus... Horner syndrome... Cushingoid features

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: Which of the following lymph node regions, when found to be enlarged during the clinical examination of a patient with suspected malignancy, is most classically associated with the spread of an intra-abdominal primary tumor?
options: The epitrochlear lymph nodes near the distal arm
The inguinal lymph node chain located in the groin
The supraclavicular lymph node in the neck area
The axillary lymph node group in the upper limb
The cervical lymph node chain in the lateral neck
correctOption: The supraclavicular lymph node in the neck area
optionExplanations: Epitrochlear nodes are associated with infections or lymphomas of the upper limb and are not typical for cancer spread.
Inguinal nodes usually drain the lower limbs and perineal area, not primarily intra-abdominal viscera.
The supraclavicular node (specifically the left side, often called Virchow's node) is a classic site for metastatic spread from abdominal malignancies.
Axillary nodes typically drain the breast and upper limbs, rather than abdominal primary sites.
Cervical nodes are more commonly associated with head and neck cancers or lymphomas rather than abdominal primaries.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [Clinical examination of the cancer patient] Lymph nodes... Supraclavicular

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 58-year-old male with a significant smoking history presents with progressive puffiness of the face and a sensation of 'fullness' in the head that worsens when he leans forward. Physical examination reveals non-pulsatile distension of the jugular veins. Which physiological mechanism best explains the aggravation of his symptoms during stooping?
options: Increased back-flow pressure arising from cerebral edema
Sympathetic denervation leading to decreased vascular tone
Increase in intracranial pressure due to arterial hypertension
Reduced venous return from the lower limbs to the right atrium
Compression of the carotid arteries by a mediastinal mass
correctOption: Increased back-flow pressure arising from cerebral edema
optionExplanations: In Superior Vena Cava Obstruction (SVCO), the lack of drainage leads to back-flow pressure and cerebral edema, which is worsened by gravity during stooping.
This describes Horner syndrome, which might co-exist with lung cancer but does not explain the postural aggravation of facial swelling.
The symptoms are venous in origin, not related to systemic arterial hypertension.
Stooping primarily affects upper body venous pressure in the context of SVCO, not lower limb return.
Carotid compression would lead to ischemic symptoms rather than venous distension and facial edema.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 142 (Book Page): Headache secondary to cerebral oedema arising from the back-flow pressure may also occur and tends to be aggravated by bending forwards, stooping or lying down.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: When differentiating between causes of neurological deficits in a patient with spinal metastases, which clinical finding is specifically characteristic of Cauda Equina compression rather than a Spinal Cord (conus) lesion?
options: Asymmetrical sensory loss following a radicular pattern
Increased knee and ankle reflexes with extensor plantars
Symmetrical and profound weakness of the lower limbs
Early and severe loss of bladder and rectal sphincter tone
Presence of a definitive and symmetrical sensory level
correctOption: Asymmetrical sensory loss following a radicular pattern
optionExplanations: Cauda equina involves individual nerve roots, leading to asymmetrical sensory loss and radicular pain patterns.
Increased reflexes (upper motor neuron signs) indicate spinal cord involvement, whereas cauda equina shows lower motor neuron signs.
Symmetrical and profound weakness is more characteristic of spinal cord compression.
Early sphincter loss is characteristic of conus medullaris lesions; cauda equina often spares sphincters until late stages.
A sensory level is pathognomonic for a spinal cord lesion, as it indicates a complete horizontal block.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 141 (Book Page): [Box 7.13] Cauda equina... Weakness: Asymmetrical... Sensory loss: Asymmetrical, radicular pattern... Sphincters: Often spared

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 66-year-old male with a history of metastatic prostate cancer presents with a 48-hour history of severe mid-back pain that he describes as a 'tight band' around his chest. He reports that the pain is significantly worse when he is lying flat or coughing. On examination, he has 3/5 power in his legs bilaterally and diminished pin-prick sensation below the level of the umbilicus. What is the most immediate priority in the clinical management of this suspected condition?
options: Initiation of high-volume intravenous saline to treat suspected dehydration
Immediate surgical consult for radical prostatectomy to reduce tumor load
Ordering an isotope bone scan to evaluate for widespread lytic lesions
Continuous intravenous infusion of broad-spectrum antibiotics for sepsis
Prompt administration of high-dose glucocorticoids like dexamethasone
correctOption: Prompt administration of high-dose glucocorticoids like dexamethasone
optionExplanations: Dehydration is not the primary concern in MSCC; fluid management is for hypercalcemia or sepsis.
Prostatectomy is not the treatment for MSCC; focal decompression of the spine is the surgical goal.
While bone scans detect metastases, MRI is the diagnostic gold standard for visualizing cord compression.
The presentation is neurological/compressive, not infectious; antibiotics are not the priority.
High-dose steroids are the first-line emergency management to reduce edema around the spinal cord while awaiting imaging or surgery.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 141 (Book Page): Malignant spinal cord compression is a medical emergency and should be treated with analgesia and high-dose glucocorticoid therapy (Box 7.14).

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: During a musculoskeletal assessment of a patient with a suspected bronchial malignancy, the clinician notes significant tenderness upon palpation of the wrists. Which of the following conditions is most likely being manifested in this clinical presentation?
options: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy associated with lung cancer
Peripheral neuropathy resulting from the secretion of ectopic hormones
Metastatic infiltration of the carpal bones from a primary lung lesion
Systemic bone resorption due to parathyroid hormone-related protein
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome causing secondary joint inflammation
correctOption: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy associated with lung cancer
optionExplanations: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA) is a classic sign of lung cancer presenting as wrist tenderness and finger clubbing.
Peripheral neuropathy causes sensory/motor changes in a 'glove and stocking' distribution, not localized joint tenderness.
Bone metastases usually affect the axial skeleton (pelvis, spine) rather than the small bones of the wrist.
PTHrP causes hypercalcemia and generalized bone pain, but HPOA is the specific cause of wrist tenderness in lung cancer.
Lambert-Eaton affects the neuromuscular junction causing proximal muscle weakness, not wrist tenderness.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Wrist tenderness (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy)

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: An umbilical nodule discovered during the abdominal examination of a patient with suspected malignancy is a classic clinical sign that suggests which of the following?
options: Primary melanoma of the abdominal wall skin
Metastatic spread from a gastrointestinal cancer
Direct invasion of the bladder into the umbilicus
Superior vena cava obstruction with collateralization
A benign hernia resulting from increased ascites
correctOption: Metastatic spread from a gastrointestinal cancer
optionExplanations: Primary melanoma can occur anywhere, but an umbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) is classically metastatic.
Sister Mary Joseph nodules are umbilical metastases classically associated with intra-abdominal or pelvic malignancies.
While bladder cancer exists, the umbilicus is specifically linked to peritoneal or GI spread.
SVCO collateral vessels appear on the chest wall, not as a discrete umbilical nodule.
While hernias occur with ascites, a solid nodule suggests malignancy (metastasis) rather than just a hernia sac.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Abdomen... Umbilical nodule... [Page 150 (Book Page)] nodules in the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph nodules).

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 72-year-old female is evaluated for suspected ovarian carcinoma. On assessment, she is found to be capable of performing all her self-care activities but is unable to carry out any work-related tasks. She spends approximately 6 hours of her 16-hour waking day resting in a chair. How would her ECOG Performance Status be classified?
optionExplanations: Grade 3 requires the patient to be confined to a bed or chair for more than 50% of waking hours.
Grade 4 describes a completely disabled patient totally confined to a bed or chair.
Grade 2 applies to patients capable of self-care but unable to work, who are up more than 50% of waking hours (10 hours up vs 6 hours resting).
Grade 1 allows for light work or sedentary occupation, which this patient cannot do.
Grade 0 requires being fully active and able to carry on all usual activities without restriction.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 138 (Book Page): [Box 7.6] 2: Ambulatory and capable of all self-care but unable to work. Up and about more than 50% of waking hours

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 52-year-old female with metastatic breast cancer to the bones is brought to the clinic by her family. They report she has been increasingly drowsy and 'not herself' for three days. She complains of persistent nausea and has been drinking excessive amounts of water and urinating frequently. Her skin is dry with poor turgor. Which metabolic sign of malignancy is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Hypokalemia due to ectopic ACTH production
Hypocalcemia due to osteoblastic bone lesions
Hyperuricemia from rapid tumor cell turnover
optionExplanations: Hypercalcemia is common in breast cancer and causes 'stones, bones, abdominal moans, and psychic groans' (polyuria, nausea, drowsiness).
Hypokalemia causes muscle weakness and arrhythmias, not typically the polyuria/polydipsia seen here.
Hyponatremia (SIADH) typically presents with fluid overload or neurological symptoms, not dehydration/polyuria.
Hypocalcemia causes tetany and seizures, the opposite of the drowsiness and polyuria described.
Hyperuricemia (Tumor Lysis Syndrome) primarily causes renal failure and electrolyte shifts like hyperkalemia, not the specific calcium triad.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 143 (Book Page): [Hypercalcaemia of malignancy] Clinical features... include drowsiness, delirium, nausea and vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia and dehydration.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: The production of which biologically active substance is most commonly responsible for the development of hypercalcemia in a patient with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung?
optionExplanations: PTHrP is the primary mediator of humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy, particularly in squamous cell carcinomas.
Vasopressin (ADH) leads to hyponatremia (SIADH), also more common in SCLC.
ACTH production leads to Cushing's syndrome, classically in small cell lung cancer (SCLC).
FGF-23 production is associated with hypophosphataemic osteomalacia in mesenchymal tumors.
Erythropoietin leads to polycythemia and is associated with renal or hepatic tumors, not lung squamous cell cancer.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 143 (Book Page): [Hypercalcaemia of malignancy] It is most commonly due to over-production of PTHrP (80%)... [Page 144 (Book Page) Box 7.18] PTHrP... NSCLC (squamous cell)

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: Which of the following physical signs, if identified during the respiratory examination of a patient with suspected thoracic malignancy, would point specifically toward a diagnosis of lung cancer over other mediastinal masses?
options: Visible distension of the veins on the chest wall
Puffiness and cyanosis of the face and neck
Dullness to percussion at the base of the lung
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side
Finger clubbing observed during hand inspection
correctOption: Finger clubbing observed during hand inspection
optionExplanations: Chest wall vein distension is a sign of SVCO, which can be caused by any mediastinal mass (lymphoma, etc.).
Facial puffiness and cyanosis are also generic signs of Superior Vena Cava Obstruction, not specific to lung cancer.
Dullness at the base suggests pleural effusion, which can occur in many cancers and non-malignant conditions.
Tracheal deviation occurs with any large mass or significant pleural effusion and is not specific to lung cancer.
Finger clubbing is a highly characteristic sign of bronchogenic carcinoma among thoracic malignancies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Finger clubbing in lung cancer

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 64-year-old woman with a history of progressive abdominal distension and weight loss is found to have a palpable nodule at the umbilicus during physical examination. What is the most likely clinical significance of this finding?
options: Inflammatory reaction to a peritoneal cyst
Direct extension of a primary renal tumour
Superficial obstruction of the biliary duct
Tethering of the skin from a breast lesion
Metastatic spread from an ovarian carcinoma
correctOption: Metastatic spread from an ovarian carcinoma
optionExplanations: While inflammation can cause umbilical changes, in a patient with weight loss and distension, a nodule is highly suspicious for malignancy.
Renal masses typically present as palpable masses in the flanks rather than nodules localized at the umbilical site.
Biliary obstruction typically presents with jaundice (icterus) and pruritus rather than a localized umbilical nodule manifestation during examination.
Skin tethering is a characteristic sign associated with breast cancer, but it occurs over the breast tissue, not at the umbilicus.
Nodules at the umbilicus, known as Sister Mary Joseph nodules, are classic signs of peritoneal deposits, commonly from ovarian or gastrointestinal malignancies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 150 (Book Page): Occasionally, peritoneal deposits are palpable as an omental ‘cake’ and nodules in the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph nodules).

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A patient diagnosed with a mediastinal mass presents with facial swelling and distended neck veins. During the assessment, which postural change is most likely to aggravate the patient's headache?
options: Walking at a brisk and continuous pace
Standing upright from a sitting position
Bending forwards or stooping down lower
Rotating the neck toward the right side
Sitting with the legs elevated on a chair
correctOption: Bending forwards or stooping down lower
optionExplanations: Walking is not a specific aggravating factor for the venous congestion headache associated with superior vena cava obstruction.
Standing upright typically reduces intracranial pressure and would likely alleviate rather than aggravate a headache caused by venous congestion.
In SVCO, bending forward increases back-flow pressure in the venous system, worsening the cerebral oedema and the associated headache.
Neck rotation may affect local venous flow but is not the classic aggravating posture described for cerebral oedema in SVCO.
Leg elevation might increase central venous pressure slightly but bending the torso forward is the most significant aggravating maneuver for these symptoms.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 143 (Book Page): Headache secondary to cerebral oedema arising from the back-flow pressure may also occur and tends to be aggravated by bending forwards, stooping or lying down.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A clinician is differentiating between types of malignant spinal compression. Which clinical finding would most specifically suggest cauda equina compression rather than spinal cord compression?
options: Presence of an extensor plantar reflex
Early loss of urinary sphincter control
Increased knee and ankle reflex scores
Asymmetrical sensory loss in the limbs
correctOption: Asymmetrical sensory loss in the limbs
optionExplanations: An extensor plantar reflex is an upper motor neuron sign seen in spinal cord or conus medullaris compression, not cauda equina.
Early loss of sphincter control is more characteristic of conus medullaris compression, whereas in cauda equina, it is often spared.
Symmetrical weakness is more characteristic of spinal cord or conus medullaris compression rather than the cauda equina.
Increased reflexes (upper motor neuron signs) suggest spinal cord compression; cauda equina lesions typically present with decreased reflexes.
Cauda equina compression typically presents with asymmetrical findings due to the involvement of individual nerve roots rather than the cord.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 141 (Book Page): 7.13 Comparison of features of neurological deficit... Cauda equina... Weakness: Asymmetrical... Sensory loss: Asymmetrical, radicular pattern.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 68-year-old man with known metastatic prostate cancer presents with a 48-hour history of severe back pain that he describes as a 'tight band' around his chest. The pain is noticeably worse when he lies flat or coughs. On examination, he has reduced sensation in both legs and difficulty initiating urination. His vital signs show a blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg, pulse 82 bpm, and temperature 37.1°C. What is the most likely diagnosis indicated by these clinical features?
optionExplanations: The 'band-like' pain, aggravation by lying flat/coughing, and dermatomal sensory loss are pathognomonic clinical features of malignant spinal cord compression.
Vertebral osteitis (infection) would typically present with significant fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and less likely acute neurological deficit levels.
Acute transverse myelitis can cause similar signs but is less likely than malignancy-related compression in a patient with known prostate cancer.
Epidural hematoma typically has a hyperacute onset and is usually associated with trauma or coagulopathy rather than gradual progressive cancer pain.
Cauda equina presents with asymmetrical signs and lower motor neuron findings, whereas 'band' pain and level-based sensory loss suggest cord involvement.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 141 (Book Page): The earliest sign is back pain, often rapidly worsening or in a ‘band’, most marked on coughing and lying flat. Subsequently, sensory changes develop in dermatomes below the level of compression, and motor weakness distal to the block occurs.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: During the monitoring of a patient receiving erlotinib for lung adenocarcinoma, the clinician identifies painful inflammation around the fingernails and deep cracks at the fingertips. These clinical signs are most characteristic of which drug class toxicity?
optionExplanations: VEGF inhibitors are more commonly associated with hand-foot syndrome (erythrodysesthesia) and hypertension rather than paronychia.
PD-1 inhibitors (immunotherapy) usually cause maculopapular rashes or autoimmune-like dermatitis rather than localized paronychia.
Paronychia and fingertip cracks are specific and high-yield dermatological signs associated with EGFR inhibitors like erlotinib.
HER2 inhibitors are primarily associated with cardiomyopathy and do not typically manifest with specific fingertip cracks or nail inflammation.
Alkylating agents typically cause generalized skin drying or alopecia rather than specific paronychia and fingertip-localized cracking.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment... Paronychia – EGFR inhibitors... Finger tip cracks – EGFR inhibitors.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: According to the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status scale, a patient who is capable of only limited self-care and is confined to a bed or chair for more than 50% of waking hours is classified as which grade?
optionExplanations: Grade 0 signifies a patient who is fully active and able to carry on all usual activities without any restriction.
Grade 4 signifies a completely disabled patient who cannot carry out any self-care and is totally confined to a bed or chair.
Grade 1 describes a patient restricted in strenuous activity but ambulatory and able to carry out light work.
Grade 2 applies to patients who are ambulatory and capable of self-care but up and about more than 50% of waking hours.
Grade 3 specifically defines a patient confined to a bed or chair for more than 50% of the day and only capable of limited self-care.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 137 (Book Page): 7.6 Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status scale... 3 Capable of only limited self-care, confined to bed or chair more than 50% of waking hours.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with chronic cough, hemoptysis, and right-sided miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis. These neurological signs on his face are most likely associated with a malignancy in which anatomical location?
options: The superior segment of the lower lobe
The mid-portion of the thoracic esophagus
The lateral lobe of the thyroid gland
The bifurcation of the main bronchus
The apex of the lung (Pancoast tumor)
correctOption: The apex of the lung (Pancoast tumor)
optionExplanations: Tumors in the lower lobes are too distal to affect the sympathetic ganglia located near the superior thoracic inlet and neck.
Esophageal tumors may cause dysphagia or laryngeal nerve palsy (hoarseness) but do not typically cause facial Horner syndrome.
While thyroid masses can compress local structures, Horner syndrome is a classic board association for lung cancer examination findings.
Tumors at the bronchial bifurcation typically cause cough or superior vena cava obstruction but rarely involve the cervical sympathetic chain.
The triad of miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis (Horner syndrome) indicates sympathetic nerve involvement, common in apical lung tumors.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Clinical examination of the cancer patient... Observation... Face... Horner syndrome.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 70-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is brought to the clinic by her family, who report she has become increasingly drowsy and confused over the past three days. She complains of generalized abdominal pain and persistent constipation. On examination, she appears severely dehydrated with a dry tongue and poor skin turgor. Her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg and pulse is 95 bpm. Which metabolic clinical sign should be prioritized for evaluation in this patient?
options: Arterial blood gas for lactate levels
Serum glucose and ketone body levels
optionExplanations: Potassium abnormalities primarily cause arrhythmias or muscle weakness rather than the classic constellation of constipation and severe polyuria-induced dehydration.
Drowsiness, confusion, constipation, and dehydration are the classic 'stones, moans, groans, and psychiatric overtones' of hypercalcemia, common in breast cancer.
Hyponatremia (SIADH) causes confusion and seizures but typically presents with normovolemia or hypervolemia rather than severe dehydration and constipation.
Lactic acidosis presents with tachypnea and signs of shock; while it can cause confusion, it does not explain the prominent gastrointestinal symptoms.
Diabetic emergencies can cause confusion and dehydration, but the specific finding of severe constipation points more strongly toward hypercalcemia.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 144 (Book Page): Hypercalcaemia of malignancy... Clinical features: The symptoms of hypercalcaemia are often non-specific and may mimic those of the underlying malignancy. They include drowsiness, delirium, nausea and vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia and dehydration.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: In a patient with bulky lymphoma undergoing their first cycle of chemotherapy, which biochemical finding is recognized as the earliest marker of tumor lysis syndrome?
optionExplanations: Hypocalcemia occurs as a consequence of hyperphosphatemia in tumor lysis syndrome but is not typically the very first marker to rise.
Pre-treatment LDH is a marker of tumor burden and risk assessment rather than a marker of the acute lysis event itself.
As cancer cells lyse, potassium (the primary intracellular cation) is released into the bloodstream, making it the earliest detectable biochemical marker.
Hyperuricemia is a key feature of the syndrome due to nucleic acid breakdown, but potassium is generally released first from the cytosol.
Hyperphosphatemia occurs early due to the release of intracellular phosphates, but serum potassium is cited as the earliest biochemical indicator.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 144 (Book Page): Tumour lysis syndrome... Investigations and management: Elevated serum potassium may be the earliest biochemical marker but pre-treatment serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) correlates with tumour bulk.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 58-year-old man presenting for evaluation of a suspicious lung lesion is noted to have significant wrist tenderness upon palpation. What specific clinical entity is most likely represented by this sign?
optionExplanations: Dermatomyositis presents with skin rashes (Grotton papules) and muscle inflammation rather than isolated skeletal wrist tenderness.
HPOA is a classic paraneoplastic sign associated with lung cancer, manifesting as finger clubbing and painful wrist/long bone tenderness.
Lambert-Eaton is a paraneoplastic syndrome causing proximal muscle weakness, not localized wrist bone tenderness.
Cerebellar degeneration presents with ataxia and gait disturbances rather than skeletal or joint-specific tenderness during a physical exam.
Neuropathy causes sensory loss or paresthesias; bone tenderness is characteristic of periosteal reaction in syndromes like HPOA.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Clinical examination of the cancer patient... Skeletal survey... Wrist tenderness (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy).

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: During a routine physical examination of a 62-year-old woman with a history of vague abdominal discomfort and bloating, a firm, non-tender nodule is palpated at the umbilicus. This specific physical finding is most strongly associated with which of the following underlying conditions?
options: Localized lymphatic drainage from a breast malignancy
Metastatic infiltration from a primary ovarian carcinoma
Primary subcutaneous deposition of a follicular lymphoma
Superficial spread of a primary basal cell carcinoma
Inflammatory extension of a complicated diverticulitis
correctOption: Metastatic infiltration from a primary ovarian carcinoma
optionExplanations: Breast cancer typically metastasizes to axillary nodes, bone, or lung; umbilical involvement is rare and not the classic association.
Nodules in the umbilicus, known as Sister Mary Joseph nodules, are clinical signs of metastatic intra-abdominal malignancy, classically ovarian or gastrointestinal cancers.
Follicular lymphoma typically involves systemic lymphadenopathy rather than isolated umbilical nodules associated with peritoneal spread.
Basal cell carcinoma typically presents as a skin lesion, not a deep umbilical nodule signifying internal malignancy.
While inflammation can cause umbilical changes, a firm nodule in a patient with abdominal symptoms is pathognomonic for metastatic cancer.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 150 (Book Page): Occasionally, peritoneal deposits are palpable as an omental ‘cake’ and nodules in the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph nodules).

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 65-year-old male smoker presents with a persistent cough and a new-found aching in his wrists and ankles. On examination, there is marked finger clubbing and exquisite tenderness upon palpation of the distal radius and ulna. What is the most likely pathological mechanism for these skeletal findings?
options: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy secondary to lung cancer
Direct metastatic infiltration of the distal long bone periosteum
Paraneoplastic secretion of calcitonin leading to osteoblastic activity
Acute urate crystal deposition following spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome
Secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic vitamin D deficiency
correctOption: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy secondary to lung cancer
optionExplanations: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA) is a syndrome of clubbing and periostitis of distal long bones, frequently associated with lung cancer.
Metastases usually cause focal bone pain in the spine or pelvis rather than symmetrical distal wrist tenderness and clubbing.
Calcitonin is a marker for medullary thyroid cancer and does not typically cause this clinical triad of clubbing and wrist pain.
Tumor lysis syndrome causes renal failure and electrolyte disturbances rather than chronic clubbing and periosteal wrist tenderness.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism causes diffuse bone resorption and metabolic bone disease, not localized wrist tenderness with clubbing.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Wrist tenderness (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy)

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A patient with a known mediastinal mass presents with facial plethora, distended non-pulsatile neck veins, and upper limb edema. Which clinical sign most reliably distinguishes this presentation from right-sided heart failure?
options: The absence of respiratory distress when the patient is lying flat
The detection of a systolic murmur loudest at the apex of the heart
The occurrence of cyanosis strictly localized to the perioral region
The presence of bilateral peripheral pitting edema in the lower limbs
The finding of a non-pulsatile, elevated jugular venous pressure
correctOption: The finding of a non-pulsatile, elevated jugular venous pressure
optionExplanations: Both SVCO and heart failure can present with dyspnea aggravated by lying flat; it is not a distinguishing feature.
Systolic murmurs are indicative of valvular disease and do not help differentiate the cause of venous congestion in the neck.
Cyanosis in SVCO involves the face and upper extremities, not just the perioral region, due to venous stasis in the drainage area of the SVC.
Lower limb edema is common in heart failure but usually absent in isolated Superior Vena Cava Obstruction.
In SVCO, the JVP is elevated but non-pulsatile because the obstruction is proximal to the right atrium, blocking the transmission of atrial waves.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 142 (Book Page): Elevated, non-pulsatile jugular venous pulse (66%)

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 72-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer reports a 'band-like' pain around his mid-thorax for three days. Today, he notes difficulty walking and 'pins and needles' in both feet. On examination, he has 3/5 power in his legs bilaterally and a sensory loss to light touch beginning at the level of the umbilicus. What is the most likely anatomical level of the spinal cord compression?
optionExplanations: C4 compression would cause quadriplegia and sensory loss from the neck down, not the umbilicus.
The umbilicus is the landmark for the T10 dermatome. Sensory loss starting here indicates compression of the cord at or above the T10 level.
L2 compression (cauda equina or conus medullaris) would cause sensory loss in the groin/thighs, not a level at the umbilicus.
S5 involvement would cause 'saddle' anesthesia in the perianal area, not a transverse sensory level at the abdomen.
T6 sensory level would be at the level of the xiphoid process, significantly higher than the umbilicus.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 140 (Book Page): The earliest sign is back pain, often rapidly worsening or in a ‘band’... Subsequently, sensory changes develop in dermatomes below the level of compression.

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A patient undergoing targeted therapy for advanced lung cancer develops a painful acneiform rash on the face and upper trunk, along with brittle finger tip cracks. Which drug class is most classically associated with these specific cutaneous clinical signs?
options: Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) inhibitors
optionExplanations: VEGF inhibitors are more commonly associated with hypertension and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, not acneiform rashes.
PARP inhibitors typically cause hematological toxicities like neutropenia and anemia rather than the described skin findings.
EGFR inhibitors classically cause acneiform rashes and skin toxicities like paronychia and fingertip cracks due to the high expression of EGFR in skin cells.
CDK4/6 inhibitors are primarily associated with neutropenia and gastrointestinal side effects rather than specific acneiform skin changes.
HER2 inhibitors are most noted for cardiotoxicity; while skin changes can occur, the acneiform rash/fingertip crack complex is specific to EGFR inhibitors.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): Acneiform rashes – EGFR inhibitors... Finger tip cracks – EGFR inhibitors

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 78-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is assessed in clinic. She spends approximately 10 hours of her 16-hour waking day resting in a chair because she lacks the energy for self-care, though she can still walk to the bathroom independently. According to the ECOG Performance Status scale, what is her current grade?
optionExplanations: Grade 2 describes patients ambulatory and capable of all self-care but up and about more than 50% of waking hours.
The patient is in a chair for 10/16 waking hours (62.5%), which is >50%. Grade 3 applies when a patient is confined to bed or chair more than 50% of the time.
Grade 1 applies to patients restricted in strenuous activity but ambulatory and able to carry out light work.
Grade 4 signifies a patient who is completely disabled, unable to carry out any self-care, and totally confined to bed or chair.
Grade 0 signifies a patient who is fully active and able to carry on all usual activities without restriction.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 138 (Book Page): 3 Capable of only limited self-care, confined to bed or chair more than 50% of waking hours

category: Identify important clinical signs in patients with cancer
statement: A 58-year-old male heavy smoker presents with drooping of the left eyelid and a constricted left pupil. On physical examination, the left side of his face is found to be drier than the right. Which of the following is the most likely clinical interpretation of these findings in the context of oncology?
options: Superior vena cava syndrome causing localized facial edema and nerve compression
Ectopic production of ACTH causing focal Cushingoid changes
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome causing asymmetric ocular muscle weakness
Metastatic infiltration of the cranial nerves within the cavernous sinus
Horner syndrome due to an apical lung tumor involving the sympathetic chain
correctOption: Horner syndrome due to an apical lung tumor involving the sympathetic chain
optionExplanations: SVCO causes bilateral facial plethora and venous distension rather than unilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.
Ectopic ACTH causes systemic signs like moon face and buffalo hump (Cushingoid features), not localized eyelid drooping or miosis.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome causes proximal muscle weakness and autonomic dysfunction, but it is typically symmetric and affects limbs more than causing isolated Horner syndrome.
Cavernous sinus involvement usually affects multiple cranial nerves (III, IV, VI) causing ophthalmoplegia, not just isolated Horner syndrome.
The triad of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis constitutes Horner syndrome, often caused by a Pancoast tumor invading the sympathetic trunk in the neck.
